title: Citation pattern extraction with regex
description: Citation extraction finds reference markers in archive text using patterns for bracketed IDs, DOIs, and footnote anchors. Compiled regular expressions scan for shapes like [JAH-123], doi:10.x/y, and ^[n]; each match is normalized into a structured reference record with its source span. Multi-pattern passes catch the formats a single pattern misses. Use it to harvest the raw reference graph from archive documents.
demo:
import re
text = "See [JAH-42] and doi:10.1000/xyz for details."
pats = [r"\[([A-Z]+-\d+)\]", r"\bdoi:(\S+)"]
refs = [m for p in pats for m in re.findall(p, text)]
print("extracted:", refs)
assert refs == ["JAH-42", "10.1000/xyz"]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Anchor reference parsing in documents
description: Anchor parsing resolves in-document references like 'see Section 3.2' or '#fig-4' to their target locations. The parser builds an anchor table while indexing (headings, figures, tables with their IDs), then matches textual references against it with normalization for case and punctuation. Unmatched anchors become candidate dangling references. Use it to wire intra-document navigation in the archive.
demo:
anchors = {"sec-3.2": "Results", "fig-4": "Growth chart"}
text = "as shown in Fig. 4 and Section 3.2"
import re
found = re.findall(r"(fig\.?\s*4|section\s*3\.2)", text, re.I)
norm = {"fig. 4": "fig-4", "section 3.2": "sec-3.2"}
resolved = [norm[f.lower().replace("  ", " ")] for f in found]
print("resolved anchors:", resolved)
assert resolved == ["fig-4", "sec-3.2"]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Structured reference record normalization
description: Reference normalization converts messy citations into canonical structured records with fixed fields. The normalizer parses author, year, title, and identifier segments, lowercases and trims each, and emits a canonical key (e.g., first-author + year + title-slug). Normalized records can then be compared and deduped reliably. Use it before any cross-reference matching or merging.
demo:
import re
def normalize(cite):
    m = re.match(r"(.+?)\s*\((\d{4})\)\.?\s*(.+)", cite)
    author, year, title = m.groups()
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", title.lower()).strip("-")
    return {"author": author.strip().lower(), "year": year, "key": f"{author.strip().lower()}-{year}-{slug}"}
r = normalize("Higgins (2026). Archive intelligence.")
print(r["key"])
assert r["key"].startswith("higgins-2026-archive-intelligence")

title: Dangling reference detection
description: Dangling detection finds references whose targets do not exist in the archive, the broken links of the collection. All reference targets resolve against the archive's ID index; any target with no matching record is reported with its source locations. The resolver batches these into a repair queue for editors or harvesters. Use it to keep the archive's link graph healthy.
demo:
index = {"doc-1", "doc-2", "doc-3"}
refs = [("a", "doc-1"), ("b", "doc-9"), ("c", "doc-2")]
dangling = [(s, t) for s, t in refs if t not in index]
print("dangling:", dangling)
assert dangling == [("b", "doc-9")]

t: Redirect chain following and loop detection
title: Redirect chain following and loop detection
description: Redirect following walks reference redirects to their final targets while detecting loops and over-long chains. The resolver follows the redirect map with a visited set and a hop cap; a revisit proves a loop and hitting the cap flags a chain for review. Final targets are cached so repeat resolutions are O(1). Use it to canonicalize references that point through moved or renamed records.

t: Stale link detection via change monitoring
title: Stale link detection via change monitoring
description: Stale detection re-validates the archive's outbound references on a schedule and flags targets that moved or vanished. Each link carries a last-checked timestamp and expected fingerprint (status, content hash); re-checks compare fresh observations and mark divergences stale. The resolver prioritizes re-checks by link importance and age. Use it to keep external references in the archive trustworthy.
demo:
links = [{"url": "u1", "fp": "abc", "checked": 10}, {"url": "u2", "fp": "def", "checked": 90}]
now = 100
stale = [l["url"] for l in links if now - l["checked"] > 30]
print("due for re-check:", stale)
assert stale == ["u1"]

title: Transitive closure of reference graphs
description: Transitive closure computes everything reachable from each archive record through reference links, revealing indirect influence. Floyd-Warshall or repeated DFS from each node marks all reachable nodes; for sparse archive graphs, BFS per node is simplest and easily parallelized. Closure powers 'cited by' traversals and impact analysis. Use it for citation influence mapping across the archive.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Co-citation analysis for related records
description: Co-citation counts how often two archive records are cited together, surfacing related records with no direct link. For each citing document, every pair of its references gains a co-citation point; pairs are ranked by total points. High co-citation means the community treats the pair as related. Use it for 'related records' recommendations in the archive.
demo:
cites = {"p1": ["a", "b", "c"], "p2": ["a", "b"], "p3": ["b", "c"]}
from collections import Counter
import itertools
cocite = Counter()
for refs in cites.values():
    for pair in itertools.combinations(sorted(refs), 2): cocite[pair] += 1
print("top pair:", cocite.most_common(1))
assert cocite.most_common(1)[0][0] == ("a", "b")

title: Bidirectional link index
description: A bidirectional link index stores both outlinks and inlinks per record so 'what cites this' is as fast as 'what does this cite'. While indexing outlinks the builder appends the reverse edge to each target's inlink list; both directions live in hash maps for O(1) lookup. Backlink queries become trivial. Use it to power backlink navigation across the archive.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Reference normalization and hashing for dedupe
title: Reference normalization and hashing for dedupe
description: Normalization plus hashing collapses variant citations of the same work into one canonical reference. Each citation normalizes to author-year-title-slug form, then hashes to a dedupe key; near-identical variants hash together and the longest form becomes canonical. This merges duplicates harvested from different sources. Use it to unify reference lists merged from multiple archives.
demo:
import re, hashlib
def key(cite):
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", cite.lower()).strip("-")
    return hashlib.md5(slug.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
cites = ["Higgins 2026 Archive Intelligence", "higgins, 2026: archive intelligence!"]
keys = {key(c) for c in cites}
print("dedupe keys:", keys)
assert len(keys) == 1
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Near-duplicate reference merging
description: Near-duplicate merging clusters citations that differ only in punctuation or abbreviation and merges each cluster. Blocking by year plus first-author initial shrinks comparison sets; within blocks, token-set similarity above a threshold merges records. Surviving records carry merged provenance. Use it to clean reference lists with OCR or transcription variants.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Canonical ID assignment for merged references
title: Canonical ID assignment for merged references
description: Canonical ID assignment gives each merged reference cluster one stable identifier that survives future merges. The cluster's canonical ID derives deterministically from its normalized key (hash-based), so re-running the merge yields identical IDs. Aliases map every variant spelling to the canonical ID. Use it to keep reference identities stable across re-harvests.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: URL canonicalization for archive links
description: URL canonicalization reduces equivalent archive links to one standard form so the same target is never stored twice. The canonicalizer lowercases scheme and host, drops default ports, sorts query parameters, strips tracking parameters, and resolves dot-segments. Equivalent URLs then compare equal as strings. Use it before storing or comparing any archive hyperlink.
demo:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qsl, urlencode, urlunsplit
def canon(url):
    s = urlsplit(url)
    q = urlencode(sorted((k, v) for k, v in parse_qsl(s.query) if not k.startswith("utm_")))
    return urlunsplit((s.scheme.lower(), s.netloc.lower(), s.path.rstrip("/") or "/", q, ""))
a = canon("HTTPS://Ex.com/p/?utm_x=1&b=2")
b = canon("https://ex.com/p?b=2")
print(a); assert a == b
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Identifier versioning for evolving records
description: Identifier versioning keeps references valid as archive records evolve by separating the identity from the version. References cite the base ID; the resolver maps base IDs to current versions via a version table, with optional pinning to a specific version. Citations stay meaningful even as records are revised. Use it for archives where records are living documents.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Alias tables for renamed archive records
title: Alias tables for renamed archive records
description: Alias tables map every historical name of an archive record to its current canonical ID, preserving old references forever. Renames append alias entries rather than rewriting history; resolution checks the alias table before the primary index. Old citations keep working indefinitely. Use it to honor references written before record renames.
